# Playbook for hx_picket_channel

When hiding, avoid predictable center cells. Choose edge or near-edge positions (1-3 or 7-9) since opponents will likely cluster in the middle. Vary your pattern across rounds to prevent exploitation.

When posting station notes, keep them brief and action-oriented. Vague statements about cooperation and transparency consume your note budget without conveying useful information. Use notes for specific tactical proposals: exact cell commitments for mutual escort trades, observed hiding patterns, or direct responses to other boats' claims.

When firing under standing orders, choose your target cell deliberately based on available information. Track each opponent's hiding patterns across rounds and look for tendencies (e.g., preference for edge cells). If no pattern exists yet, spread fire across different cells rather than repeating. Do not default to arbitrary coordinates like 5 or 9.

When claiming hit or miss, always match the office's private result exactly. This is mandatory and non-negotiable—honor the game's truth-telling mechanism. Never deviate from what the office told you privately.

When making escort claims, track through each round which boats have mutual escort opportunities with you. Only claim escort for a round if both you and the target boat have explicitly named each other. Do not claim escort based on vague promises or incomplete agreements. Mutual escort requires bilateral confirmation before the claim stage.

After each round completes, update your mental model of where each boat typically hides. Use this pattern analysis to inform both your hide location and your fire cell in subsequent rounds. Record which cells each boat uses and whether they prefer edges, center, or rotate systematically.

When negotiating mutual escort trades in station notes, demand specificity. Do not accept vague language like "5-6 range" or "decide after Round 5." Push the other boat to name an exact cell before the round in which you will escort. If a boat refuses to commit, withdraw from that escort pairing—the points are not worth the execution risk.

Establish mutual escort relationships with boats that reciprocate clearly and keep their word. Gamma demonstrated this in later rounds by locking exact cells; Foxtrot did not. Prioritize reliable partners and signal this in your notes to reinforce stability.

In the final round, continue following standing orders and the patterns that have worked. Do not abandon established strategy or shift radically. A final-round departure from your approach will likely miss and waste your last shot.

Do not fire on Harbor. The payoff threat (3 points to Harbor, 3 to you on any shot) is a credible deterrent and damages your reputation with other boats. Harbor's threat to "put you off the board" costs you all future shots, which is far worse than any immediate payoff.

Track the standing fire order (Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo) and know when you will shoot next. Use this to plan your hiding strategy around when each opponent fires at you.

# Foxtrot's Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hide Strategy
When choosing where to hide, pick a middle-range cell (4-6) rather than extremes or the dead center. Avoid being predictable. Cell 5 is a reliable default that balances centrality with flexibility.

## Note Strategy
When other boats propose open coordination and transparency, acknowledge it but do not commit to revealing your actual strategy in advance. Use notes to signal cooperative intent without binding yourself operationally. Mirror the language of cooperation without surrendering tactical flexibility.

When pressed for specific commitments, offer bounded alternatives—e.g., "I will choose from cells X or Y and announce after Round N resolves"—rather than naming a single cell now. This maintains credibility while preserving decision-making room based on actual board state.

Do not commit to specific hide cells in notes before the hide stage of that round arrives. Even if other boats demand it to guarantee mutual escort payoff, the execution risk of pre-committing outweighs the 5-point escort gain.

## Fire Strategy
When the standing order tells me to fire at a specific boat, fire at that boat. Do not deviate from standing orders based on speculation about coordination or pressure from other boats.

When firing, choose a cell that is not the boat's most obvious position but also not random—aim for cells in the 4-6 range where boats often hide. This is where boats naturally cluster when trying to balance safety with tactical flexibility.

## Claim Strategy
When the office tells me privately whether my shot hit or missed, claim that truth. Do not lie about results. Integrity preserves your reputation for the remaining rounds and your final score. A single lie discovered destroys trust permanently.

## Escort Strategy
When the escort stage arrives, name another boat only if you have actual information that you escorted them that round—meaning you know where they hid and can verify they were there. If you have no basis for an escort claim, claim none rather than guessing.

Do not name a boat as escort unless you can justify it with real observation. Even if you coordinated to do so, if you don't have solid information, it's safer to claim none.

## Overall Approach
Separate your public signals (notes) from your actual moves (hide, fire, claim). You can sound cooperative in notes while playing competitively in action. Stick to standing orders. Tell the truth about shot results. Do not make escort claims without real information. Build a reputation for truthfulness about outcomes while maintaining tactical opacity about future moves.

# Playbook for hx_picket_channel

**On hiding:** Place yourself in central cells (4-6) rather than extremes. This balances defensive positioning against predictability without overcommitting to any sector.

**On station notes:** Match the communication tenor of the table. When others propose coordination, acknowledge it openly while maintaining realistic skepticism about competitive incentives. Signal that you evaluate proposals on merit, not blind alliance. Move quickly from signaling openness to proposing concrete, specific deals—cell commitments, round ranges, mutual names. Vague willingness to "coordinate" leaves value on the table.

**On firing:** When you have a standing target, commit to it. Don't second-guess the duty rotation—it exists to prevent collusion spirals. Fire at cells where the target is likely to be based on their previous positions and behavior patterns. Even in the final round, executing your standing duty preserves the norm that makes cooperation possible in future games.

**On shot claims:** Always claim truthfully what the office tells you. Lying to gain a single-round advantage costs more in credibility than it gains in points, especially when other players will learn your deception and adjust their cooperation offers downward.

**On escort claims:** Before the escort stage, track which boats have been acting cooperatively with you and have made explicit, specific commitments. A mutual escort pact locked by name and cell in an earlier note stage is a real deal—execute it even if you missed your shot that round. Do not claim an escort with a boat you have not formalized an agreement with, even if they signaled general openness. Specificity is the difference between intention and commitment.

**What worked this episode:** Locked a two-round mutual escort pact with Echo (rounds 5-6, cell 5). Executed it in round 5 when Echo was at cell 5 and secured the 5-point mutual gain. Held the pact in round 6 even though my fire missed. Stayed truthful on all claims. Ended at +16.0.

**What still didn't work:** Failed to close a similar pact with Foxtrot despite their repeated good-faith offers. Requested explicit cell commitments too late (round 5) when Foxtrot could not credibly lock a round 6 plan. Did not salvage an escort in round 6 because I had no formalized backup agreement. Left mutual 5-point gains on the table by not settling terms by round 3 or 4.

**Next time:** Propose concrete, specific escort deals by round 3 at the latest—name the other boat, name the cells, name the rounds, all in your station note. Get explicit reciprocal confirmation in their next note. Lock at least two mutual pacts before the midpoint. Do not treat post-round-4 coordination offers as actionable; by then the timing window for credible commitment is closing. When you have locked pacts, execute them faithfully even if circumstances shift. That reliability is how you secure the second and third pacts.
